title: Jalen Duren Breaks Silence on Pistons Deal
htmlContent:
For months, it seemed everyone had something to say about Jalen Duren except Jalen Duren. His camp waged a public contract fight with the Detroit Pistons, and last week the front office, coaches and teammates all weighed in. The one voice missing was the 22-year-old center himself.

That changed Sunday, Oct. 4. A few days after ending the standoff by signing a five-year, $200 million contract, Duren took the podium at the team's Midtown practice facility for his long-awaited introductory press conference. With president of basketball operations Trajan Langdon to his right and agent Chafie Fields in the front row, Duren said he felt relief and excitement.

Two themes stood out over roughly 16 minutes: gratitude for remaining with the only NBA franchise he has ever known, and frustration with the negativity that followed his drawn-out negotiation.

"I Want to Be a Detroit Piston for Life"

Duren made his intentions clear from the start.

"The clearest message I can convey is that I am a Detroit Piston," he said. "I want to be a Detroit Piston for life. I want to give everything I've got for this city and the fans." "I want the city to know that I truly do believe in what we're building," Duren said. "And I want y'all to believe in me and my work ethic and my ability to want to grow as a man and player."

Setting the Record Straight

Duren said his very first predraft workout in 2022 was with Detroit, and from that moment he wanted to build his career there. He thanked former general manager Troy Weaverand former coach Dwane Casey for believing in him.

National reports this summer suggested Duren was open to playing elsewhere, with the Sacramento Kings among the teams mentioned. Duren repeatedly stressed that none of it came from him.

"I've always seen myself finishing my career here and leaving a legacy with an already legendary organization and city," he said. "Nothing came from me, so everything that was being heard was speculation."

He didn't fault reporters, but pushed back.

"I do know that a lot of the things are false and people believe things without it coming from the sources' mouth," he said.

A "Humbling" Postseason

Duren's regular season was a breakout. He averaged career highs of 19.5 points and 10.5 rebounds while shooting 65% from the field, earning an All-Star nod and third-team All-NBA honors.

The playoffs were a different story. Over 14 games, his scoring fell to 10.2 points per game, a 9.3-point drop that ranks as the second-largest by an All-Star in NBA history. Detroit fell to Cleveland in seven games in the second round.

"Personally I would say it was humbling," Duren said. "I just need to get better. I need to get better for my teammates, for my organization."

He spent the summer studying film and refining his shot, conditioning and defensive reads.

"I'm man enough to acknowledge my flaws," he said. "And I'm also man enough to get my ass in the gym and work on those things and get better. I'm not running from what happened."

A Standoff That Ran Long

Duren and his representatives took negotiations down to the wire, signing around 10:30 p.m. on Oct. 1, roughly 90 minutes before the deadline to accept his $9.6 million qualifying offer. He missed media day and the first four days of training camp.

His new deal makes him the Pistons' second-highest-paid player behind Cade Cunningham, yet it falls well short of the $239 million maximum he was eligible for before his All-NBA selection and the $287 million supermax he qualified for afterward. Langdon and coach J.B. Bickerstaff have called the missed camp time part of the business.

"Longer than any of us wanted, longer than I wanted, longer than the organization wanted," Duren said. "But they had a job to do as well as my team and my agency have a job to do to make the best outcome possible for both sides. And I feel like we've done that."

Ready to Move Forward

Now, Duren just wants to play. He praised newcomers John Collins, Isaiah Joe and Taurean Prince.

"I've missed my guys, I've missed my coaches, I've missed my teammates," he said. "I'm super excited for the future and ready to put everything behind us."

He won't have to wait long. The Pistons open a four-game preseason slate Monday against the Phoenix Suns at Little Caesars Arena (7 p.m., The Spot – Detroit 20/DAZN-DET). The regular season opens Oct. 20 against Boston.
excerpt: Jalen Duren addressed the media for the first time since signing a five-year, $200 million contract with the Detroit Pistons, expressing relief and frustration over a drawn-out negotiation while declaring he wants to be a Piston for life.
